name: Esther Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. My mother says I shouldn't talk to strangers about money, so I'll keep it general where I can.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for my uncle's building firm in our market town, five of us including him. We do house extensions, porches, a barn conversion now and then, and repairs on the church hall roof whenever the parish finds the money. I'm on the carpentry side, studwork, joists, fitting windows, and I'm still slow at it because I came to it late after leaving school and working in a café. I love when an old couple brings out tea and tells you about the house; I hate the paperwork my uncle leaves on the van seat.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Tomas, he's a mechanic at the tractor dealer, and we're getting married in the parish church next June. We live in a rented cottage on the farm road, and we've got maybe three weeks of money saved, most of it already promised to the wedding. My uncle pays fair, but there's not much building round here beyond him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it. At church people would agree with me, I think. I don't go online much, so nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same worries as now. My uncle's sixty-one and talks about slowing down, and if my uncle stops there's no firm. That's my job, gone, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and learn as much as I can from my uncle while he's still at it. Tomas and I would keep the wedding small, the church and the hall, no fancy hotel. I'd ask my uncle straight out what his plans are, which I've been putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, quietly. More about my uncle than about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have you put off asking your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's family, and you don't ask a man when he's going to stop. My aunt would think I was after the firm. I'm not, I just want to know if I'll have a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your uncle did retire, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a bigger firm in the next town, but they mostly hire lads with papers. I'd probably have to go back to the café while I sorted something. That would sting.

say: I'd say I **never trusted** AI in the first place.
I'd expect people at **church** to agree with me.
think: Her uncle is **sixty-one** and talks about slowing down.
If he stops, there's **no firm** and no job, AI or not.
do: Learn all she can from her **uncle** while he's working.
Keep the **wedding small**: church and hall, no hotel.
Ask her uncle directly about his **retirement plans**.
feel: **Quietly worried**, more about her **uncle** than computers.

fieldNote: Her real risk is **family succession**, not technology.

steps.text: Learn joists and window fitting from her uncle while he works
Hold the wedding in the church and hall, not a hotel
Ask her uncle when he plans to stop running the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices, but people round here still want a builder they know. At work my uncle would say the same. At church we'd talk about the young ones losing office jobs in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it barely touches us for a while, because we're small and everything is different. But my uncle might use it to price jobs and send letters, and then he might not need my cousin in the office. She does the books two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, to be honest. I won't use the apps myself, my uncle can do that if he wants. Tomas and I would put a little aside each month after the wedding, maybe a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for my cousin than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your cousin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn the new programme before my uncle does, so she's the one who runs it. She's cleverer than me with computers. I'd hate to see family pushed out by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it barely touches you. Is that true for the bigger firm in the next town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, probably not. They'd use all of it, and bid cheaper than my uncle on extensions. That's the bit that could hurt us, now I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, and I'd pray it's not true. At church we'd say God didn't make people to be idle. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it would finish my uncle's firm within a few years. By 2028 the big firms price everything by computer and undercut him, and by 2031 their robots build the extensions. I'd be thirty-one with no papers and possibly a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle to keep me on as long as he can, and I'd stick with him. Tomas and I might wait on children, which I'd hate. I'd lean on the church and the family; we look after our own here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the floor's going and I can't see where to step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned possibly a baby. How would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wanted to start soon after the wedding. If this happened, Tomas would say wait, and I'd cry about it, and then agree. That's the part I couldn't stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn or change, with three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd learn. Everything I'd learn, the robot would learn faster. Maybe I'd help with the old buildings, church roofs, the things a robot can't fit up a narrow lane.

I'd say at church that God didn't make people to be **idle**.
think: By 2028 **big firms** undercut her uncle, and by 2031 their robots build.

**Delay children** with her fiancé, much as she'd hate it.
Lean on **church and family** for support.

She can't see a **skill** worth learning, which deepens her alarm.

steps.text: Stay at her uncle's firm for as long as he keeps her on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and the church and the town should start thinking. At work my uncle would say he'll be retired by then anyway. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years till robots is better, but my uncle would retire in that time anyway. So the question is still who employs me, just with a bit more warning. I'd have to find out if I can take over the old-building work somehow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle to teach me the church and listed-building work, the lime and oak and old joints, because that's where a person still matters. I'd keep spending low. And I'd see whether the bigger firm needs anyone for heritage jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can see a little path through the old buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider going back to college for papers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it was something real like heritage carpentry. Not a computer course. I'm not moving away from my family, so any course has to be near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd back me. He's worried about tractors with no drivers anyway. We'd have to plan things together, which we're not very good at.

say: I'd say the **church and town** should start thinking now.
My uncle would joke he'll be **retired by then** anyway.
think: **Eight years** is better, but her uncle retires in that time anyway.
The real question is **who employs her** next.
do: Ask her uncle to teach her **heritage carpentry**: lime, oak and old joints.
Ask the **bigger firm** about heritage jobs.
feel: **Worried**, but she sees a **little path** through old buildings.

fieldNote: She pins hope on **heritage work** with old buildings.

steps.text: Learn lime, oak and old joint work from her uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so don't panic. At church I'd say we should trust in God and work hard. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until robots, I'd be forty. My uncle would long be retired, and I'd hope to be doing heritage work. Maybe even running a small crew with my cousin doing the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle about taking over part of the firm, the heritage side, over five years. I'd go to the college for a heritage carpentry course near home. Tomas and I would start a family when we planned, without waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but a normal kind of worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a normal kind of worried. What's normal for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bills, the wedding, my uncle. Same as now. Robots that far away I'd leave to God.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work with their hands and know their neighbours. I'd also make sure they could use whatever the computers are by then. I wouldn't want them left behind like I might be.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so don't panic.
At church I'd say to **trust in God** and work hard.
think: By forty her uncle would be retired and she'd hope for **heritage work**.
She might run a **small crew** with her cousin doing the books.
do: Ask her uncle about taking over the **heritage side** over five years.
Take a **heritage carpentry** course near home.
Start a **family** on their own timeline.
S4.quote: Robots that far away I'd leave to God.
fieldNote: A decade restores her **family plans** and heritage hopes.
She leaves distant risk to **faith**.

steps.text: Take a heritage carpentry course at the local college

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My uncle's firm would go, we'd put off children, and I wouldn't know what to learn. What would help is a heritage carpentry course near home, and maybe some support for small family firms so the big ones don't swallow them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. If the young ones all leave for work, there's no one to fill the church or fix its roof. I'd like to stay and be the one who fixes it.

headlineQuote: If the young ones all leave for work, there's no one to fill the church or fix its roof.
portrait: Esther is **27**, a junior carpenter in her **uncle's small firm**, engaged and saving for a June wedding.
She's **traditional**, churchgoing, avoids AI and leans on family rather than the state.
Her steady worry is her uncle's **retirement**, which could end her job in any scenario.
AGI by **2028** alarms her because she can't see a skill robots won't copy.
With more time she hopes to take on **heritage work** on old buildings near home.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her uncle's firm gone and children **delayed**.
whatWouldHelp: A **heritage carpentry** course near home and support for **small family** firms.
